title: Minimal Mathlib Imports for Elementary Proof
content: The proof uses only Nat.Prime, Nat.factorial, ZMod, and Tactic — a remarkably small import footprint for a theorem about prime distributions. No analytic number theory (complex analysis, L-functions, sieve methods) is needed.
mathContext: Key Mathlib facts: $\text{Nat.exists\_prime\_and\_dvd}: n \geq 2 \Rightarrow \exists p$ prime with $p \mid n$. $\text{Nat.dvd\_factorial}: p$ prime, $p \leq n \Rightarrow p \mid n!$. These two elementary facts are the only number-theoretic tools beyond basic arithmetic.

title: Multiplicativity of Residue 1 (mod 3)
content: mul_mod_three_one: the product of two integers ≡ 1 (mod 3) is ≡ 1 (mod 3). Proved directly from Nat.mul_mod and computation. This is the group property of (ℤ/3ℤ)* — the multiplicative group of a field — applied to the identity element 1.
mathContext: $(a \cdot b) \bmod 3 = ((a \bmod 3) \cdot (b \bmod 3)) \bmod 3 = (1 \cdot 1) \bmod 3 = 1$. More generally, $(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^* = \{1, 2\}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$; this is the closure property under multiplication by 1.

title: Primes Other Than 3 Are ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 3)
content: Every prime p ≠ 3 satisfies p % 3 ∈ {1, 2}. The proof rules out p % 3 = 0 by noting that 3 | p implies p = 3 (since p is prime), contradicting p ≠ 3. The remaining cases 1 and 2 follow by omega. This is the starting point for the classification of prime factors.
mathContext: Primes $p \neq 3$ in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$: $p \not\equiv 0$ (else $3 \mid p$, forcing $p = 3$). So $p \equiv 1$ or $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. Combined with mul_mod_three_one: the only way a product can be $\equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ is if at least one factor is $\equiv 2$.

title: factors_determine_mod_three and has_prime_factor_2_mod_3
content: factors_determine_mod_three: if all prime factors of n are either 3 or ≡ 1 (mod 3), then n ≢ 2 (mod 3). Proved by strong induction. The inductive step extracts a prime factor p ≡ 1 (mod 3), divides n = p·m, uses mul_mod to show m ≡ 2 (mod 3), then applies the inductive hypothesis to m < n. has_prime_factor_2_mod_3 is the contrapositive: n ≡ 2 and n ≥ 2 implies a prime factor ≡ 2 exists.
mathContext: Strong induction: $n = p \cdot m$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, $m < n$. Then $n \equiv p \cdot m \equiv m \pmod{3}$, so $m \equiv 2$ and we recurse to $m$. Contrapositive: $n \equiv 2 \Rightarrow \exists p \mid n$ prime with $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$.

title: The Euclid-Style Construction N = 3·(n+1)! - 1
content: Given any n, construct N = 3·(n+1)! - 1. Then: (1) N ≡ 2 (mod 3) since 3 | 3·(n+1)!, so N ≡ -1 ≡ 2 (mod 3). (2) N has a prime factor p ≡ 2 (mod 3) by has_prime_factor_2_mod_3. (3) p > n: if p ≤ n+1, then p | (n+1)! (by Nat.dvd_factorial), so p | 3·(n+1)!, but also p | N, giving p | 1, contradiction. Therefore p > n is a prime ≡ 2 (mod 3) larger than n.
mathContext: $N = 3 \cdot (n+1)! - 1 \equiv -1 \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. Size argument: $p \leq n+1 \Rightarrow p \mid (n+1)! \Rightarrow p \mid 3(n+1)! \Rightarrow p \mid (3(n+1)! - N) = 1$, contradicting $p$ prime. So $p > n$.

title: Set-Theoretic and Order-Theoretic Reformulations
content: primes_2_mod_3_infinite packages the result as Set.Infinite for {p prime | p % 3 = 2}, using Set.infinite_of_not_bddAbove. no_largest_prime_2_mod_3 gives the order-theoretic version: there is no maximum element. Both are immediate corollaries of infinitely_many_primes_2_mod_3.
mathContext: Equivalences: $\{p \text{ prime} : p \equiv 2\}$ is infinite $\iff$ unbounded $\iff$ no maximum. The three formulations cover set-theoretic, order-theoretic, and combinatorial uses of the result.

title: Concrete Examples: 2, 5, 11, 17, 23
content: Five concrete witnesses: 2, 5, 11, 17, 23 are all primes congruent to 2 mod 3. Verified by decide or rfl. The sequence continues: 29, 41, 47, 53, ... These are OEIS A003627 (primes of the form 3n-1).
mathContext: First primes $\equiv 2 \pmod{3}$: $2, 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 41, 47, \ldots$ By Dirichlet's density theorem, they comprise exactly $1/\phi(3) = 1/2$ of all primes (asymptotically).
